source: Read a rocket's velocity-time graph: the slope is acceleration, the area is height, and the top of the flight is where the line crosses zero.
Students think the rocket is highest where the velocity graph is highest, at burnout, instead of where velocity reaches zero.

From the story. The boys launched rocket after rocket from Cape Coalwood, their name for an old slack dump outside town. A graph turns the numbers from a flight into a picture you can read at a glance. (More in October Sky.)

A velocity-time graph tells the whole story of a straight-up flight. While the motor burns, the line climbs. After burnout, gravity alone acts, so the line falls at a steady slope of $-9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. The rocket is still going up until that line reaches zero.

On a velocity-time graph: slope = acceleration, area between the line and the time axis = displacement (height gained), and apogee is where $v = 0$. For a straight-line boost from rest to $v_b$ at $t_b$, then a coast, the whole area to apogee is one triangle: $h = \tfrac12 v_b\,t_\text{top}$.
The green line is velocity. The shaded area so far is the height gained. The top of the flight is where the line crosses zero, not at burnout.
Velocity rises in a straight line to $60\ \text{m/s}$ at $t = 2\ \text{s}$, then coasts. Find the time of apogee and the height reached.
After burnout, $v$ falls $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ each second: $60/9.8 = 6.12\ \text{s}$ more, so apogee is at $t = 8.12\ \text{s}$.
Thinking the rocket is highest at burnout because that's where the velocity graph peaks. The velocity is highest there; the height keeps growing until velocity reaches zero.
